newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate to target Superfund, brownfields.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate to target Superfund, brownfields.

text.p: Overhaul of the Superfund hazardous waste cleanup program and redevelopment of abandoned industrial sites will have top billing in the Senate's agenda, Senate aides and industry officials said Friday.
Republican Sen. John Chafee plans to introduce a bill Tuesday to revise the Superfund program and Sen. Frank Lautenberg plans to introduce a bill on brownfields.

Lautenberg's bill, among the first 10 that Democratic leaders will introduce this year, would provide additional grants to state and local governments to assess brownfield sites, a spokesman for the New Jersey Democrat said.

It would provide funds for low interest loans to current owners of the properties, prospective purchasers and municipalities to clean up contaminated sites to clear the way for redevelopment, spokesman Ken Jakes said.
The bill would also relieve from cleanup liability prospective buyers who did not cause the contamination or took reasonable precautions to reduce the problem.
Details on Chafee's proposal, set to be among the first bills that the Senate Republican leadership would introduce Tuesday, were not available.

A Superfund bill offered last year by Republican Sen. Bob Smith of New Hampshire stalled in a battle with the administration over relieving companies that dumped toxic waste legally before 1981 from having to pay to clean it up.

Clinton administration officials said recently that they no longer saw a need for a major legislative overhaul of the Superfund program, because their administrative reforms had improved the pace and reduced the cost of cleanups.
As Superfund talks on the House side fell apart last year, the administration proposed narrower brownfield reforms as a compromise.
Lautenberg's introduction of a brownfields bill did not necessarily indicate he would oppose broader reform of the toxic waste cleanup law, Jakes said.
While not pursuing broad Superfund changes, the administration is looking to reinstate Superfund taxes which expired at the end of 1994.
Republicans last year said they would not approve renewal of the taxes without reforms in the Superfund program.

Without new taxes, the Superfund coffers would be drained by 2000, assuming the government spent about $1.34 billion a year for cleanup operations, according to a report by the Congressional Budget Office last year.
